AB acoustic clan

Prince William Sound
discrete calls
Communication

Consists of calls shared between AB, AI, AJ and AN pods, distinct from calls shared by coresident pods in the AD clan of southern Alaska resident killer whales

Vertical: Inferred yesHorizontal: Inferred yesOblique: Unclear
Evidence and details

Description: Consists of calls shared between AB, AI, AJ and AN pods, distinct from calls shared by coresident pods in the AD clan of southern Alaska resident killer whales

Vertical: "the most parsimonious explanation for the existence of vocal clans is that killer whale calls are socially learned from maternally related individuals" (Yurk et al. 2002)

Horizontal: "If vertical cultural transmission from mother to offspring were the only mechanism responsible for the transmission of call types, one should also see minor variations among calls produced by different matrilines However, as Deecke et al. (2000) have shown such variation only occurs in structurally simpler call types, while complex call types remain highly similar among matrilines of the same pod. Therefore, vertical cultural transmission also cannot be the only mechanism for the observed repertoire differences" (Yurk et al. 2002)

Domains: communication

Avacha acoustic clan

Avacha Gulf, Kamchatka, Sea of Okhotsk
discrete calls
CommunicationSocial

Pulsed calls that are one of the vocalizations produced by killer whales alongside whistles and echolocation.

Recorded from 2001 to 2006
Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Pulsed calls that are one of the vocalizations produced by killer whales alongside whistles and echolocation. "Most killer whale pulsed signals fall into discrete call types with higher or lesser variability inside them (Ford 1984)....The fact that all of the discrete calls of Southeast Kamchatka resident killer whales can be divided into several distinctive structural classes suggests that they have some rules defining the structure of the calls. These rules are not common for killer whales as a whole. For example, calls of transient killer whales from Southeast Kamchatka and killer whales from Sakhalin region do not obey these rules. Thus these rules are presumably the cultural tradition of Southeast Kamchatka resident killer whales...The acoustic markers of community membership - in the case of Southeast Kamchatka killer whales, with phonotactics - could help prevent the division of the community and, hence, a loss of potential mates if we assume that "vocal tradition" is a cultural tradition applied to vocal behaviour, then, to a great extent, all resident killer whales from Southeast Kamchatka share the same vocal tradition. Still, some of them share no call types, and, following Ford's (1991) definition of "clan", belong to different clans." (Filatova et al. 2007). "The dialect of each group always contains Biph l class calls and squeak-like Moph l class calls. Besides this, all groups from Avacha clan produce Biph 2 class calls, and some of them additionally produce Moph 2 class calls." (Filatova et al. 2007, p. 270).

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: suspected unknown

Domains: communication; social

Crozet Island killer whales

Crozet Archipelago
longline depredation
Foraging

Crozet killer whale ecotypes habitually remove Paragonian toothfish caught on commercial fishery longlines around Crozet Islands in Southern Ocean from fishery establishment in 1996

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: YesOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Crozet killer whale ecotypes habitually remove Paragonian toothfish caught on commercial fishery longlines around Crozet Islands in Southern Ocean from fishery establishment in 1996

Horizontal: Depredation behavior spread from 7 to 17 social units from 2005 to 2014. Social network analysis indicated best-fitting was the “model assuming social transmission and incorporating demographic processes as covariates…our findings also suggest that horizontal social transmission was initially the prevalent learning pathway, with approximately 40% and 60% of the killer whale social units being estimated as having acquired the depredation behaviour independently and from their preferential associates at the unit level, respectively…Evidence of social units independently acquiring the depredation behaviour in our study suggests that in certain units, the individual initially learning depredation did so without direct social interactions with individuals from other social units. Within these units, the behaviour likely indeed originated from an innovator before spreading among members via observation or imitation” (Auguin et al. 2025)

Domains: foraging

Anthropogenic effects: Whales are feeding on human fishery longlines and fishers sometimes kill whales in retaliation, leading to population decline around early 2000s, although behavior has continued spreading (Auguin et al. 2025)

Sources: [3]

Northern Resident killer whales

Johnstone Strait
whistles
CommunicationSocial

Whistles are a form of underwater communication distinct from pulsed calls; for Northern Residents used mainly during socializing in close physical proximity. Stereotyped whistles are

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Whistles are a form of underwater communication distinct from pulsed calls; for Northern Residents used mainly during socializing in close physical proximity. Stereotyped whistles are "repetitive with a distinct spectrographic contour". Unlike other delphinids which use signature whistles for individual identification, orcas have stable matrilines without dispersal and used in short-range rather than long-range communication, so "group identity encoded in stereotyped signals is probably more important than the individual identity of the group members" and individuals from different matrilines use the same whistle types (Riesch et al. 2006).

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: "Vocal learning is the most probable mechanism behind vocal mimicry (Ford, 1991, Janik and Slater, 1997) as well as horizontal transmission of discrete calls in wild killer whales (Deecke et al. 2000). We believe our results provide evidence that stereotyped whistles are also learned." Findings that whistle types changed in WG from 1970s to 1990s in the A-clan and long lifespans of whales indicates learning continues into adulthood and during socializing with other clans (Riesch et al. 2006)

Oblique: suspected unknown

Domains: communication; social

Anthropogenic effects: noise from sea vessels

Sources: [4]

Resident killer whales

Gulf of Alaska, Aleutian Islands, Bering Sea; northern North Pacific
groundfish depredation
ForagingSocial

Resident (R-type) killer whales in the North Pacific primarily eat fish; depredation of groundfish from longline fisheries.

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Resident (R-type) killer whales in the North Pacific primarily eat fish; depredation of groundfish from longline fisheries. "Analysis of the associations between n = 532 whales seen on more than one occasion revealed one large network of 441 (83 %) connected individuals, and some peripheral groupings comprising 91 individuals that were unconnected to the large network...We hypothesize that depredation behavior is likely first spread within groups of consistent associates (likely matrilines) and then spread to associating groups that may witness depredation during these associations. During this study, we observed large aggregations of whales (max encounter group size = 120) likely composed of multiple matrilines traveling and feeding together (median encounter group size = 15, consistent with a single matriline; see Matkin et al. 1999; Ford et al. 2000)" (Fearnbach et al. 2014)

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: "At a larger scale, the four defined clusters were linked by occasional associations to form a single large connected network, with an expansive longitudinal range (ca. 3,000 km)...the large connected network may facilitate the spread of information throughout the population by cultural transmission...We hypothesize that depredation behavior is likely first spread within groups of consistent associates (likely matrilines) and then spread to associating groups that may witness depredation during these associations. During this study, we observed large aggregations of whales (max encounter group size = 120) likely composed of multiple matrilines traveling and feeding together (median encounter group size = 15, consistent with a single matriline; see Matkin et al. 1999; Ford et al. 2000)" (Fearnbach et al. 2014)

Oblique: suspected unknown

Domains: foraging; social

Anthropogenic effects: depredation of fish from human fishing lines; effects unclear but may lead to conflict with humans?

selective foraging
Foraging

Resident killer whales feed primarily on Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) and other salmonids, in contrast to Transient (T-type) which specialize in mammals. “Killer whale populations in other regions, such as Norway, Argentina and Antarctica, also specialise on particular prey types…Such...

Vertical: Inferred yesHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Resident killer whales feed primarily on Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) and other salmonids, in contrast to Transient (T-type) which specialize in mammals. “Killer whale populations in other regions, such as Norway, Argentina and Antarctica, also specialise on particular prey types…Such specialisations appear to represent behavioural traditions that are passed across generations by social learning (Guinet & Bouvier 1995, Ford et al. 1998, Saulitis et al. 2000), and have been described as cultures (Rendell & Whitehead 2001)…The disproportionate occurrence of chinook salmon in prey samples relative to its low abundance led Ford et al. (1998) to suggest that resident killer whales may forage selectively for this species over other available salmonids…​​The known distribution patterns of resident killer whales are consistent with what would be expected of a predator focused on chinook salmon” (Ford & Ellis 2006)

Vertical: inferred due to matrilineal structure

Domains: foraging

Anthropogenic effects: Population mortality linked with abundance of Chinook salmon, which declined in 1990s possibly due to El Niño conditions. “This stress, potentially acting synergistically with immunosuppressive effects of the high levels of polychlorinated biphenyls and related pollutants found in these whales (Ross et al. 2000), resulted in increased susceptibility to disease and higher mortality rates.” Behavioral specialization in prey despite biological capacity for generalized diet may endanger population. (Ford et al. 2010)

Sources: [6] [7]

porpoise harassment
SocialPlay

Harassment defined as interacting with porpoises in ways that could injure or kill them. From 1962 to 2020, documented 78 incidents of Salish Sea SRKW harassing porpoises, including 28 suspected or likely kills, but porpoises were never eaten. Harassment observed across all three pods (J, K, and L)...

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Harassment defined as interacting with porpoises in ways that could injure or kill them. From 1962 to 2020, documented 78 incidents of Salish Sea SRKW harassing porpoises, including 28 suspected or likely kills, but porpoises were never eaten. Harassment observed across all three pods (J, K, and L) and evenly males and females, both juveniles and adults, and tended to involve more than one orca, including from different matrilines. Authors theorize practice hunting or playing (Giles et al. 2024)

Vertical: "Porpoise harassment and killing behavior was transmitted within matrilines, the tightest social unit of SRKW society. Most porpoise harassment incidents were observed involving individuals from three L pod and four J pod matrilines. Within these matrilines, many younger individuals engaged in the behavior multiple times and across years, suggesting the behavior is repeated and retained within matrilines over time" (Giles et al. 2024)

Horizontal: "Within this population, porpoise harassing or killing behavior possibly originated with L pod and was later spread to or was adopted by K and J pods" (Giles et al. 2024)

Oblique: suspected unknown

Domains: social; play

Description: Most common type of killer whale vocalization are pulsed calls, which are one of stereotyped discrete, variable, or aberrant. Discrete stereotyped broadband calls “Killer whales maintain contact with conspecifics using stereotyped broadband calls (Ford, 1989). Call types are distinguishable by the frequency modulation contours (Ford, 1989; Deecke et al., 1999; Yurk et al., 2002). Calls have the potential to convey information on signaler’s sex, matriline and pod identity, behavioral state, direction of travel, and distance relative to the receiver (Ford, 1989, 1991; Deecke et al., 2000; Miller and Bain, 2000; Miller, 2002; Nousek et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2007)” SRKW J, K, and L pods each have distinct call repertoires; transient population has single repertoire

allokelping
Social

Whales fashion short length of kelp and position it on their bodies with the help of a social partner. “After fashioning a length of kelp, the whale will then approach a partner, flip the length of kelp onto their rostrum, and press their head and the kelp against their partner’s flank. The two...

Vertical: UnclearHorizontal: UnclearOblique: Unclear
Evidence and details

Description: Whales fashion short length of kelp and position it on their bodies with the help of a social partner. “After fashioning a length of kelp, the whale will then approach a partner, flip the length of kelp onto their rostrum, and press their head and the kelp against their partner’s flank. The two whales then maneuver to keep the kelp between them while rolling it across their bodies...Whales maintained continuous contact for a median of 32 seconds during allokelping (IQR = 38; maximum = 186). During contact, whales roll and twist their bodies, often adopting an exaggerated S-shaped posture (Figure 1C). When contact is broken, the whale in the rear may retrieve the kelp and re-initiate contact” (Weiss et al. 2025)

Domains: social

Anthropogenic effects: "We hypothesize that allokelping is a cultural behavior unique to southern resident killer whales…The southern resident killer whales are critically endangered, and maintaining their ‘cultural continuity’ is a key goal under Canada’s Species at Risk Act. Declining bull kelp in southern resident killer whale habitat due to increasing temperatures may pose a threat to the persistence of this behavior" (Weiss et al. 2025)

Sources: [11]

Transient killer whales

Salish Sea
discrete calls
ForagingSocial

Most common type of killer whale vocalization are pulsed calls, which are one of stereotyped discrete, variable, or aberrant.

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Most common type of killer whale vocalization are pulsed calls, which are one of stereotyped discrete, variable, or aberrant. "The results of this study show that transient killer whales produce communicative vocalizations only extremely rarely. Transient killer whales vocalized significantly less often than residents, and for all behaviour categories except surface-active and milling after kill, the median call rate was zero." Unlike the fish preyed on by residents, the marine mammals preyed on by transients have hearing ranges that can detect killer whale calls, changing costs of vocal communication and likely explaining limited use of calls among transients. "Mammal-eating killer whales often share their prey (Jefferson et al. 1991), and sharing of prey items was common during the kills observed in this study. Vocal behaviour may be an essential part of delineating social relationships during the sharing of prey, which could also explain why it increased after a successful attack." (Deecke et al. 2005)

Domains: foraging; social

whistles
Foraging

Repertoire of three stereotyped whistles (compared with 11 or so for residents).

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Repertoire of three stereotyped whistles (compared with 11 or so for residents). "whistles of transient killer whales generally have lower dominant frequencies, narrower frequency ranges, are shorter in duration, and have fewer frequency modulations...in addition to having repertoires of pulsed calls that are distinct from residents (Ford 1984; Deecke 2003), transient killer whales also have a distinct, population-specific repertoire of whistles...rather than being the predominant acoustic signal during social interactions, transients generally do not vocalize at all except during “milling after kill” and “surface-active” behaviors (Deecke et al. 2005; this study). However, once the animals start to get vocally active both pulsed call and whistle rates increase simultaneously (Deecke et al. 2005; this study)...we hypothesize that whistles in transient killer whales may also serve as signals that facilitate and coordinate close-range interactions during surface-active behavior (similar to socializing in resident killer whales) and prey handling during feeding" (Riesch & Deecke 2011)

mammal-eating
Foraging

This ecotype seems to have a fixed preference for marine mammals as prey and have not been observed to eat fish. Mammals consumed include harbor seals (Phoca vitulina), sea lions (Zalophus californianus, Eumetopias jubatus), porpoises (Phocoena phocoena, Phocoenoides dalli) and elephant seals...

Recorded since 1987
Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: This ecotype seems to have a fixed preference for marine mammals as prey and have not been observed to eat fish. Mammals consumed include harbor seals (Phoca vitulina), sea lions (Zalophus californianus, Eumetopias jubatus), porpoises (Phocoena phocoena, Phocoenoides dalli) and elephant seals (Mirounga angustirostris) among others. They hunt cooperatively in small groups (Houghton et al. 2015)

Domains: foraging

Anthropogenic effects: In contrast to e.g. Southern residents, have increased from 1987 to 2010 and expanded feeding areas, possibly in response to increased prey abundance (harbor seals). Proposals to conserve SR whales through culling seals, which predate on salmon, are premature according to authors (Shields et al. 2018)

Social unit: Family. The basic unit is the matriline. Both sexes are philopatric (staying with natal group); males briefly disperse to mate with females in other pods in the same clan. [16]

Conservation status: Data Deficient (DD)
